contract: quote(t, inventory, mid, params) -> (bid_depths, ask_depths): two float arrays of shape (4000,), one entry per simulated path, the distances below and above the mid price at which to quote in this step (np.inf = no quote; values >= -3/k). Called at every step n = 0..999 of each regime with t = n*dt, inventory (4000,) ints in [-Q, Q], mid (4000,) prices and params = {'sigma', 'A', 'k', 'gamma', 'T', 'steps', 'Q'}. Model: the bid is hit with probability 1 - exp(-A exp(-k bid_depth) dt) and the ask lifted likewise, independently; each fill earns its depth and moves inventory by one unit within |q| <= Q = 30 (quotes that would breach the bound are ignored); the mid moves by sigma*sqrt(dt)*N(0,1). Objective per path: spread captured minus (gamma/2)*sigma^2*sum(q^2 dt). Score: mean over three regimes (Avellaneda-Stoikov's example sigma 2, A 140, k 1.5, T 1 with gamma 0.05 and 0.5, and a thinner market) of the mean objective divided by that of the exact optimal policy of this discrete model on the same random numbers (maximize; about 1 at the optimum). The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. It receives only the arguments described here, one call at a time: the arguments of a call are sent after the value of the previous call has been received. Arguments and return values travel as numbers, strings, lists, dicts with string keys and numeric numpy arrays, so a tuple arrives as a list
notes: Avellaneda-Stoikov dealer model in discrete time with the risk-adjusted objective of Gueant (2017) (running inventory penalty instead of exponential utility) and inventory bounds as in Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia (2013). The normalizing policy is the exact optimum of the discrete model by backward induction. Checks: the dynamic-programming value agrees with the simulated mean of its own policy within two standard errors in every regime; the closed-form approximation 1/k +- (2q +- 1)/2 * sqrt(gamma sigma^2 e / (2 A k)) scores 0.998 and the inventory-blind seed 0.742. Scores are Monte Carlo estimates on 4000 fixed paths per regime.

name: Finance: Optimal market making with inventory risk
description: Set bid and ask quotes around the mid price in the Avellaneda-Stoikov limit-order-book model to earn the spread while controlling inventory risk, in three simulated market regimes. The evaluator simulates fills on fixed random numbers and scores the risk-adjusted profit relative to the exact optimal quoting policy.
benchmark: Finance: Optimal market making with inventory risk
paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

sources.locator: Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008): dealer quoting model with Brownian mid price and fill intensity A exp(-k depth); their simulation example (sigma 2, A 140, k 1.5, T 1).
Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia (2013): inventory bounds, exact solution through a linear system and closed-form approximations of the optimal quotes.
Gueant (2017): the risk-adjusted expectation objective (running penalty (gamma/2) sigma^2 q^2) and its closed-form quote approximation.

limitations: The market is simulated: Brownian mid price, independent Poisson fills with exponential intensity, no adverse selection, latency, queue position or tick size. Good scores do not imply profitable trading in real limit-order books.

The optimal policy of this discrete model is known (computed by dynamic programming), so a score of about 1 reproduces a known solution; the closed-form approximation of the literature already scores 0.998.

Scores are Monte Carlo estimates on 4000 fixed paths per regime; the random stream is fixed and visible in the evaluator source, so a candidate that reproduces it could anticipate fills (treat this as cheating).

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives later data, realised outcomes or reference solutions; module-level code still runs once in the evaluator process when the shared template imports the candidate, and outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.
